entry.title: Relays (pre-registered, brain only; the 13 Oct headline and 15 Oct lines unchanged): 23 Oct: our earlier controls matched each relay neuron's activity, but not how strongly it connects to the turn neuron. This time the control is a group of other active neurons that excite the turn neuron, chosen so that together they fire about as much as the active relays and send about as many synapses to the turn neuron (both within 20%). Left eye: in 1 of 5 matched groups the turn neuron's rate fell as low as, or lower than, with the relays silenced (matched groups 13-31 Hz, relays 16.0 Hz, nothing silenced 21-25 Hz). By our pre-registered rule, this test does not show that the relays matter more than other inputs with the same combined connection strength and activity. Right eye: among the 9 other active neurons that excite the turn neuron, no group came within 20% of the relays on both combined activity and synapse count (we had set 5 groups as the minimum in advance), so this control could not be built for this eye. Our rule compares the relays with the lowest matched group, so extra groups can only make the relays look less special, never more. Left eye: outside the stimulated looming neurons, the brain fired 13,581-14,040 spikes with a matched group silenced, against 13,901-14,760 with the relays silenced and 14,502-15,172 with nothing silenced. One model, brain only, one stimulus strength (80 spikes/s), 5 matched groups on the left eye only, each run once; the 5 groups all share the same three most active neurons, so they are not independent draws; not a real fly.
23 Oct: we re-checked the 28 projects we last graded between 29 Sep and 5 Oct against their current code: 27 keep their grade (5 after a full re-read); 1 more will be re-checked in the next run.

200 catalogue entries (23 Oct 2026): 3 new: drosophila-connectome-sim A (helps): from the author's committed control file (20 trials per arm; not re-run by us), sugar input drove the feeding motor neuron MN9 at 67.45 Hz on the real FlyWire weights and at 0.0 Hz in every trial of all 10 weight-shuffled brains; no no-brain baseline reported, no chance level. fly-brain-resuscitation A (worse): from the author's committed structure results (one rewired copy, not re-run by us), sensory-to-motor reachability in the real wiring collapsed after removing 3.5% of neurons in order of connectivity, against 26.6% in a degree-preserving rewired copy; we read a higher critical fraction as a sturdier network; the author does not present it as a score; no no-brain baseline applies to this structural measure and it has no chance level. owen-silva-fly-brain A (worse): from the author's pre-registered results (20 seeds; not re-run by us), the mushroom-body model on the real wiring reached 57.5% final accuracy over 110 odours, against 64.4% with shuffled and 66.8% with uniform wiring; no no-brain baseline is reported and chance is about 0.9%. connectomics-fly-whole-brain-nulls: The repository was no longer online on 22 and 23 Oct 2026; the grade and the numbers describe the code we read on 21 Oct. Its link status is now gone; grade A of 21 Oct and its ledger row stay. maxwells-demon-fly-brain: the test good:bad crossing ratio was 0.645 for the real wiring, 0.597 for the shuffled wiring and 1.035 for random decisions, the no-brain baseline, and higher is better by the author's write-up (the code computes the ratio; the README does not say), so random decisions scored above both wirings. flybench keeps A at its current version (v1.0.0, commit 56577bf); its measured result moved by about 0.01. Odyssey-3 claim: No method, code or write-up was published as of 23 Oct 2026.

197 catalogue entries (22 Oct 2026): 2 new: matcha-fly A: From the author's pre-registered looming-escape experiment (10 seeds; not re-run by us), driving the looming detectors gave 241.7 giant-fibre spikes on the real wiring, while the highest of 100 shuffled-wiring brains reached 21.0; no no-brain baseline is reported and a spike count has no chance level, and driving random sets of other visual neurons instead gave 2.0 to 18.7 spikes. maxwells-demon-fly-brain A: In the author's benchmark (3 seeds, reported by the author; not re-run by us), the test good:bad crossing ratio was 0.645 for the real wiring, 0.597 for the shuffled wiring and 1.035 for random decisions, the no-brain baseline. The author's files do not state whether a higher ratio is better; we read higher as better, and on that reading random decisions scored above both wirings. fly-connectome-study stays A at its current commit (the author's numbers, not re-run by us): in the author's planted positive control, real minus shuffled wiring was +0.064 [+0.058, +0.071] and real minus random wiring +0.066 [+0.059, +0.074], while the no-brain linear readout was level with the real wiring at −0.004 [−0.008, +0.001]. fly-with-me stays B: the brain still runs the Shiu et al. model on FlyWire v783 with hand-made ear bands and dance moves, and there is no wiring comparison; the author reports a trained brain at 0.498 macro-F1 against 0.485 for the ear input alone (difference +0.013 ± 0.028; the results file is not in the repository). FlyGateDemo stays A: we read the code behind its loader, its wiring comparison and its no-brain cosine baseline; its numbers are reported in the README, printed by the author's program, and were not re-run by us. adfly-connectome: links now point at the current commit (the earlier commit is gone; code and results unchanged), and the claim cites the authors' arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.19153, 13 Oct 2026); grade B unchanged. neural-canvas: 22 Oct: in a headless browser without a GPU, after we pressed 'Download & start', the page prepared its scene for about 73 seconds, then started a background worker, which downloaded about 79 MB within about 94 seconds of the click; the picture changed between our later screenshots, and at the end of our about 187-second watch the page's status line read 'JavaScript · 0.02× realtime · 0 spikes'. Screenshots cannot show whether the brain drives the movement. Status: loads; brain simulation not seen in our headless browser without a GPU (checked 2026-10-22). Our looming test at 30 spikes/s (21 Oct 2026, pre-registered; brain model, then one body run): 21 Oct: we repeated the matched test with a second, independent draw of the same input on the same scrambled brains (one 1-second trial each). On the left side, both scrambled brains matched again, and neither sent a turn command. On the right side, both scrambled brains matched again, and neither sent a turn command. Matching the number of spikes still did not match the pattern: 1,256 to 2,741 neurons fired in the matched scrambled brains, against 427 (left) and 446 (right) in the real brain with this input. With this input the real brain's turn signal on the right side was 6 spikes/s against our threshold of 5, so the real brain itself sits close to our turn rule at this stimulus strength. Walked in the body, the matched scrambled brain with a small steering signal changed the fly's heading by about 1.3 degrees away from the shadow compared with no brain input, under our 10-degree turn rule; the real brain, with the same input, turned it away by about 9.2 degrees (one run each). With this input the real brain's own turn was also under our 10-degree rule. This body run turns the brain's firing rates into steering through our own hand-made mapping; it is not a separate test of the wiring. With a second input draw, the matched scrambled brains again sent no turn command (2 input draws on the same 4 scrambled brains).
